**Patrick Victor Martindale White** (28 May 1912 – 30 September 1990) was an Australian novelist and playwright who explored themes of religious experience, personal identity and the conflict between visionary individuals and a materialistic, conformist society. Influenced by the modernism of [James Joyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Joyce "James Joyce"), [D. H. Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D._H._Lawrence "D. H. Lawrence") and [Virginia Woolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Woolf "Virginia Woolf"), he developed a complex literary style and a body of work that challenged the dominant realist prose tradition of his home country, was satirical of Australian society, and sharply divided local critics. He was awarded the [Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature") in 1973 and is the only Australian to have been awarded it.[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-1)

Born in London to affluent Australian parents, White spent his childhood in Sydney and on his family's rural properties. He was sent to an English public school at the age of 13, and went on to read modern languages at Cambridge. After graduating in 1935 he embarked on a literary career. His first published novel, _[Happy Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy\_Valley\_(novel) "Happy Valley (novel)")_ (1939), was awarded the Gold Medal of the Australian Literature Society. In [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") he served as an intelligence officer in the Royal Air Force. While stationed in [Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria "Alexandria"), Egypt, in 1941, he met [Manoly Lascaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manoly_Lascaris "Manoly Lascaris"), who became his life companion and, as White later wrote, "the central [mandala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandala "Mandala") in my life's hitherto messy design."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1981100-2)

In 1948 White returned to Australia, where he bought a small farm on the outskirts of Sydney. There he wrote the two novels, _[The Tree of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tree\_of\_Man "The Tree of Man")_ (1955) and _[Voss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voss\_(novel) "Voss (novel)")_ (1957), that brought him critical acclaim in the United States and the United Kingdom. In the 1960s he wrote the novels _[Riders in the Chariot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riders\_in\_the\_Chariot "Riders in the Chariot")_ (1961) and _[The Solid Mandala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Solid\_Mandala "The Solid Mandala")_ (1966), and a series of plays, including _[The Season at Sarsaparilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Season\_at\_Sarsaparilla "The Season at Sarsaparilla")_ and _[A Cheery Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Cheery\_Soul "A Cheery Soul")_, that had a major impact on Australian theatre.

White and Lascaris moved to Sydney's [Centennial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centennial_Park,_New_South_Wales "Centennial Park, New South Wales") in 1964. From the late 1960s White became increasingly involved in public affairs, opposing the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") and supporting Aboriginal self-determination, nuclear disarmament and environmental causes. His later work includes the novels _[The Eye of the Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Eye\_of\_the\_Storm\_(novel) "The Eye of the Storm (novel)")_ (1973) and _[The Twyborn Affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Twyborn\_Affair "The Twyborn Affair")_ (1979) and the memoir _[Flaws in the Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flaws\_in\_the\_Glass "Flaws in the Glass")_ (1981)_._

## Childhood and adolescence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Childhood and adolescence")]

White was born in [Knightsbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knightsbridge "Knightsbridge"), London, on 28 May 1912. His Australian parents, Victor Martindale White, a wealthy sheep grazier, and Ruth (née Withycombe) were in England on an extended honeymoon.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr19914-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4) The family returned to Sydney, Australia, when he was six months old. As a child he lived in a flat with his sister, a nanny, and a maid while his parents lived in an adjoining flat. In 1916 they moved to a large house, "Lulworth", in [Elizabeth Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Bay,_New_South_Wales "Elizabeth Bay, New South Wales"). At the age of four White developed asthma, a condition that had taken the life of his maternal grandfather, and his health was fragile throughout his childhood.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr199127,_30%E2%80%9332-5)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Lulworth-Elizabeth-Bay-NSW-Dec-2019.jpg/250px-Lulworth-Elizabeth-Bay-NSW-Dec-2019.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lulworth-Elizabeth-Bay-NSW-Dec-2019.jpg)

Lulworth, White's childhood home in [Elizabeth Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Bay,_New_South_Wales "Elizabeth Bay, New South Wales"), Sydney

At the age of five he attended kindergarten at Sandtoft in [Woollahra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woollahra,_New_South_Wales "Woollahra, New South Wales"), close to their home. His mother often took him to plays and pantomimes and White developed a life long love of the theatre. Nevertheless, White felt closer to his nurse, Lizzie Clark, who taught him to tell the truth and "not blow his own trumpet".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr199133%E2%80%9339,_66%E2%80%9367-6)

In 1920 he attended [Cranbrook School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cranbrook_School,_Sydney "Cranbrook School, Sydney") but his asthma worsened. Two years later he was sent to [Tudor House School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudor_House_School "Tudor House School"), a boarding school in the [Southern Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Highlands_(New_South_Wales) "Southern Highlands (New South Wales)") of New South Wales, where it was thought the climate would help his lungs. White enjoyed the freedom provided by the school where discipline was lax. He read widely from the school library, wrote a play and excelled at English. In 1924 the boarding school ran into financial trouble, and the headmaster suggested that White be sent to a [public school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_school_(United_Kingdom) "Independent school (United Kingdom)") in England.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr199145%E2%80%9346,_57%E2%80%9366-7)

In April 1925 his parents took White to England to enrol in [Cheltenham College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheltenham_College "Cheltenham College") in Gloucestershire. In his first years at Cheltenham he was withdrawn and had few friends. He found his housemaster to be sadistic and puritanical, and White's certitude of his own homosexuality increased his sense of isolation. He later wrote of Cheltenham, "When the gates of my expensive prison closed I lost confidence in my mother, and [I] never forgave."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr199167%E2%80%9375,_598-8)

One of White's few pleasures was the time spent at the Somerset home of his cousin, the painter Jack Withycombe. Jack's daughter [Elizabeth Withycombe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Withycombe "Elizabeth Withycombe") became a mentor to him while he was completing his first, privately published, volume of verse, _Thirteen Poems_, written between 1927 and 1929._[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick\_White#cite\_note-NLA2-9)_[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr199182%E2%80%9385-10) White also became friends with Ronald Waterall who was two years his senior at Cheltenham and shared his passion for the theatre. He and White would spend their holidays in London seeing as many shows as they could.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr199179%E2%80%9380-11)

White asked his parents if he could leave school to become an actor. His parents compromised and allowed him to leave school without taking his final examinations if he came home to Australia to try life on the land. But their son had already changed his mind on his future profession and was determined to become a writer.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-Marr2-12)

In December 1929 White left Cheltenham and sailed to Sydney. He spent two years working as a [jackaroo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackaroo "Jackaroo") on sheep stations at Bolaro in the [Monaro district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaro_(New_South_Wales) "Monaro (New South Wales)") of New South Wales and at Barwon Vale in northern New South Wales. The landscapes impressed White and he wrote two unpublished novels during this time: "The Immigrants" and "Sullen Moon".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr199188%E2%80%93106-13)

White's uncle, who owned Barwon Vale, convinced White's parents that their son was not suited to the life of a grazier. White's mother was happy for him to become a writer but she wanted him to have a career as a diplomat as well. On this basis his parents agreed to send him to Cambridge. While studying for the entrance examinations, White completed a third unpublished novel, "Finding Heaven".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991109%E2%80%9312-14)

## Europe, America and war

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Europe, America and war")]

From 1932 White lived in England, studying French and German literature at [King's College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College,_Cambridge "King's College, Cambridge"). There he began a love affair with a fellow student that lasted until White graduated. White wrote poems, some of which were published in the [_London_ _Mercury_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Mercury "London Mercury"). He spent his holidays in France and Germany to improve his languages and read Joyce, Lawrence, [Proust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Proust "Marcel Proust"), [Flaubert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Flaubert "Gustave Flaubert"), [Stendhal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stendhal "Stendhal") and [Thomas Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Mann "Thomas Mann") with admiration. He made a pilgrimage to [Zennor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zennor "Zennor") in Cornwall where Lawrence wrote _[Women in Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women\_in\_Love "Women in Love")_ and the visit inspired further poems. A collection was published as _The Ploughman and Other Poems_ in an edition of 300 in Sydney in 1935 but received little critical attention and was later suppressed by White. A play, _Bread and Butter Women,_ was given an amateur production in Sydney the same year.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991115%E2%80%9333-15)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

On White's graduation in 1935 his mother wanted him to embark on a diplomatic career but he was determined to stay in England and become a writer. His mother relented and his father granted him an allowance of £400 a year. He moved to London's [Pimlico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pimlico "Pimlico") district where, in 1936, he met the Australian painter [Roy de Maistre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_De_Maistre "Roy De Maistre"). De Maistre briefly became White's lover and remained a mentor and friend. White later said that de Maistre had encouraged him to break from naturalistic prose and write "from the inside out."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991134%E2%80%9351-16)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

White began work on the novel _Happy Valley,_ partly based on his experience working as a jackaroo. In 1937 his story "The Twitching Colonel" was published in the _London Mercury_. His father died in December, leaving him a legacy of £10,000 that enabled him to write full-time in relative comfort. He started work on a play, _Return to Abyssinia_, and wrote skits for revues which were produced with moderate success. He completed _Happy Valley_ and the novel was accepted by the British publisher [George G. Harrap and Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_G._Harrap_and_Co. "George G. Harrap and Co.") in 1938.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991150%E2%80%93177-17)

_Happy Valley_ was published in early 1939 to generally favourable reviews which encouraged White to go to America to find a publisher there. White arrived in New York in April and travelled across the country. He visited [Taos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taos,_New_Mexico "Taos, New Mexico"), New Mexico, where he viewed Lawrence's ashes and met [Frieda Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frieda_Lawrence "Frieda Lawrence"). He then moved to [Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod "Cape Cod") where he worked on a novel, _The Living and the Dead_, partly based on his life in London. When the Second World War broke out in September, White took the first available ship back to England where he continued to work on his new novel.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991180%E2%80%9395-18)

In early 1940 White heard that Ben Huebsch, the head of the American publisher [Viking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_Press "Viking Press"), had accepted _Happy Valley_. Huebsch had published Lawrence and Joyce in America and White was delighted with the connection to these writers. Huebsch was to become one of White's main literary supporters. White decided to travel back to New York for the publication of _Happy Valley_ and to complete the new novel. Happy Valley was published in June to favourable reviews. Huebsch also accepted the now completed novel _The Living and the Dead_ for publication.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991197%E2%80%93201-19)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

White returned to London where, in November, he was called up to an intelligence unit of the Royal Air Force. He was stationed at [Bentley Priory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Bentley_Priory "RAF Bentley Priory") during the [Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blitz "The Blitz") before being transferred to North Africa in April 1941. He subsequently served in Egypt, Palestine and Greece. While stationed near Alexandria in July 1941 he met [Manoly Lascaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manoly_Lascaris "Manoly Lascaris"), who was waiting to be recruited to the [Royal Greek Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenic_Army "Hellenic Army"). Lascaris was to become White's life partner.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991205%E2%80%9306,_210%E2%80%9332-20)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

Following the war White was determined to leave England to avoid "the prospect of ceasing to be an artist and turning instead into that most sterile of beings, a London intellectual."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991236-21) White's preference was to live in Greece but Lascaris wanted to start a new life in Australia. White relented because, "It was his illusion. I suppose I sensed it was better than mine."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991241-22)

Before leaving for Australia White began work on a novel _[The Aunt's Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Aunt's\_Story "The Aunt's Story")_, inspired by a painting by Roy de Maistre. He sent the completed typescript to his American publisher in January 1947. In March, his play _Return to Abyssinia_ opened in London to polite reviews. White missed its short season because he was in Australia making preparations for his permanent return. He returned to London and began a new play, _[The Ham Funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ham\_Funeral "The Ham Funeral"),_ inspired by the [William Dobell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Dobell "William Dobell") painting "The Dead Landlord".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991249%E2%80%9352-23)

White sailed back to Australia in December 1947. During his voyage _The Aunt's Story_ was published in the United States to very favourable reviews and strong sales. Critic [James Stern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Stern_(writer) "James Stern (writer)")'s review in the _[New York Times Book Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_Book\_Review "The New York Times Book Review")_ was enthusiastic and Stern would go on to be one of White's major champions in America.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991253%E2%80%9354-24)

## Return to Australia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Return to Australia")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/%281%29Patrick_White_house_Castle_Hill-2.jpg/500px-%281%29Patrick_White_house_Castle_Hill-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:(1)Patrick_White_house_Castle_Hill-2.jpg)

White's house in Castle Hill, Sydney

White arrived back in Australia in February 1948. He and Lascaris moved to a small farm purchased by White at [Castle Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Hill,_New_South_Wales "Castle Hill, New South Wales"), now a Sydney suburb but then semi-rural. He named the house "Dogwoods", after trees he planted there. He and Lascaris worked the farm and sold flowers, vegetables, milk and cream as well as pedigree [schnauzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schnauzer "Schnauzer") puppies.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991255%E2%80%9365,_272%E2%80%9373-25)

The reviews of _The Aunt's Story_ in the British and Australian press were less enthusiastic than those in America, and White was unable to interest theatres in Australia or overseas in producing _The Ham Funeral._ He was making slow progress on the novel which was to become _The Tree of Man_ and was discouraged at his prospects of success as a writer. He also questioned his decision to return to Australia.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991258,_272%E2%80%9380-26)

In late 1951 White had a religious experience that gave him a belief in God and the inspiration to recommence work on _The Tree of Man_ (published in 1955). He described the novel as an attempt to suggest "every possible aspect of life, through the lives of an ordinary man and woman."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991281%E2%80%9383,_285-27)_The Tree of Man_ and his following work _Voss_ (1957) established White's favourable critical reputation in Britain and America. White, however, was embittered by what he considered a hostile critical response in Australia.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991305,_325%E2%80%9328-28)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

Following his international success White continued to live and work on his farm in Castle Hill. He gave few interviews and usually declined requests for public appearances, promotion of his work, and invitations for his membership of literary and cultural organisations. He entertained a close circle of friends at his home but always felt himself to be an outsider: "first as a child with what kind of strange gift no one quite knew; then a despised colonial in an English public school; finally an artist in horrified Australia."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991346%E2%80%9347,_351%E2%80%9352,_361-29)

In 1961 his novel _Riders in the Chariot_ was published, and was his first to receive almost universal critical praise in Australia.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991382-30)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4) Meanwhile, White's interest had returned to the theatre. The Drama Committee of the [Adelaide Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide_Festival "Adelaide Festival") had recommended _The Ham Funeral_ as the festival's main theatrical production for 1962. The festival governors, however, rejected the play citing concerns about "a piece of work which quite fails to reconcile poetry with social realism" and a scene involving an aborted foetus in a dustbin.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991388%E2%80%9391-31) The controversy led to a successful amateur production of the play in Adelaide followed by a professional production in Sydney. White was inspired to write three further plays which were given professional productions: _The Season at Sarsaparilla_ (1962), _A Cheery Soul_ (1963) and _[Night on Bald Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night\_on\_Bald\_Mountain\_(play) "Night on Bald Mountain (play)")_ (1964).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

In 1963 White's mother died in London and his share of the estate allowed him to buy a house in Centennial Park, near the centre of Sydney, the following year. Before leaving Dogwoods, White had bought up every copy of his early published poems he could find and burnt them along with most of his manuscripts, papers, letters and journals.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991426%E2%80%9327,_440%E2%80%9342-32)

White was working on _The Solid Mandala_, a novel about twins, Waldo and Arthur Brown, who represent contrary aspects of his own character.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991448-33) He was becoming interested in Tarot, astrology, the _[I Ching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Ching "I Ching")_ and [Jungian psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytical_psychology "Analytical psychology"), and these interests are reflected in the novel. Following its publication in 1966, White declined the Britannica Award for Literature and [Miles Franklin Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Franklin_Award "Miles Franklin Award") for the novel and stated he no longer wanted his works considered for awards.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991451%E2%80%9353,_463%E2%80%9364-34)

White had long had an interest in art and music, describing himself as "something of a frustrated painter, and a composer manqué."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991318-35) The core of his art collection was works by his friends [Sidney Nolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Nolan "Sidney Nolan") and de Maistre but he collected works by emerging Australian artists such as [James Clifford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clifford_(artist) "James Clifford (artist)"), [Erica McGilchrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erica_McGilchrist "Erica McGilchrist"), and [Lawrence Daws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Daws "Lawrence Daws") and some established artists like [Brett Whiteley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Whiteley "Brett Whiteley").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991466%E2%80%9367-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHewitt200267,_86%E2%80%9387,_92%E2%80%9393-37) In early 1967 he began work on _The Vivisector_, a novel about a painter, Hurtle Duffield, who exploits human relationships for his art. After the novel was published in 1970, Nolan believed Duffield was based on him, but White denied this, stating that Duffield was a composite of his own character and the working life of the artists [John Passmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Passmore_(artist) "John Passmore (artist)") and Godfrey Miller.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991472%E2%80%9376-38)

White was becoming more politically engaged at this time. He was opposed to Australia's involvement in the [Vietnam war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"), and in December 1969 he participated in his first political demonstration, breaking the law by publicly inciting young men not to register for military conscription. The following year he campaigned against censorship and gave evidence in favour of the publication of [Philip Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Roth "Philip Roth")'s novel _[Portnoy's Complaint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portnoy's\_Complaint "Portnoy's Complaint")_ at obscenity trials in Melbourne and Sydney. In 1972 the New South Wales government announced a plan to build an Olympic stadium near Centennial Park. White participated in the anti-development protests, giving speeches at a rally in June.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991493%E2%80%93494,_501%E2%80%93504,_508%E2%80%93510-39)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

White had been on the shortlist for the [Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature") since 1969. In 1971, after the prize was awarded to [Pablo Neruda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Neruda "Pablo Neruda"),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991532%E2%80%93534-40) he wrote to a friend: "That Nobel Prize! I hope I never hear it mentioned again. I certainly don't want it; the machinery behind it seems a bit dirty, when we thought that only applied to Australian awards. In my case to win the prize would upset my life far too much, and it would embarrass me to be held up to the world as an Australian writer when, apart from the accident of blood, I feel I am temperamentally a cosmopolitan Londoner".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1994389-41)

## Nobel laureate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Nobel laureate")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/%281%29Patrick_White_house_Centennial_Park.jpg/500px-%281%29Patrick_White_house_Centennial_Park.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:(1)Patrick_White_house_Centennial_Park.jpg)

Patrick White's home [Highbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highbury,_Centennial_Park "Highbury, Centennial Park"), in [Centennial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centennial_Park,_New_South_Wales "Centennial Park, New South Wales"), Sydney

In 1970 White had begun working on a new novel, _The Eye of the Storm_, about the meaning of his mother's death. He sent the completed work to his British publishers in December 1972. He delayed sending it to his American publishers, Viking, because _The Vivisector_ had sold poorly in America and he hoped positive reviews of the new work in Britain would increase interest in the United States.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991494,_514-42)

The novel was published in August 1973 and White was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in October. The Nobel citation praised him "for an epic and psychological narrative art, which has introduced a new continent into literature". White, pleading delicate health, declined to travel to Sweden to accept the award. Nolan attended the ceremony on his behalf.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991530,_535%E2%80%9341-43)

The Nobel prize increased worldwide interest in White's work. _Eye of the Storm_ was widely reviewed in the United States and sold 25,000 copies by March 1974. New editions of his previous novels were published and translation rights sold well. White, however, refused to have _Happy Valley_ republished as he considered it an inferior early work and he was afraid that some of the people on whom characters were based might sue for defamation.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991537%E2%80%9338,_545%E2%80%9346-44)

According to [David Marr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Marr_(journalist) "David Marr (journalist)"), White's biographer, "From the time of the prize his work became saturated with a late, relaxed sensuality."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991553-45) White himself was less relaxed about the effects of the award, telling a supporter: "the Nobel Prize is a terrifying and destructive experience."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991545-46)

White was made [Australian of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_of_the_Year "Australian of the Year") for 1973. In his acceptance speech, he said that [Australia Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_Day "Australia Day") should be "a day of self-searching rather than trumpet blowing" and that historian [Manning Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manning_Clark "Manning Clark"), comedian [Barry Humphries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Humphries "Barry Humphries") and communist trade union leader [Jack Mundey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Mundey "Jack Mundey") were more worthy of the award.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991544-47)

In May 1974 White gave a speech in support of the re-election of the [Whitlam Labor government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitlam_government "Whitlam government"), stating that it was necessary for Australia to create: "an intellectual climate from which artists would no longer feel the need to flee."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991547-48) Following a trip to [Fraser Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K'gari "K'gari") to do research for a new novel _[A Fringe of Leaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Fringe\_of\_Leaves "A Fringe of Leaves")_, he became a supporter of the campaign to stop sand mining on the island. He wrote to the re-elected prime minister [Gough Whitlam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gough_Whitlam "Gough Whitlam") on the issue and the campaign eventually forced the government to suspend its approval of mining and hold an inquiry on the matter.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991549%E2%80%9352-49)

White was among the first group of the Companions of the [Order of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Australia "Order of Australia") in 1975 but resigned in June 1976 in protest against the [dismissal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_Australian_constitutional_crisis "1975 Australian constitutional crisis") of the Whitlam government in November 1975 by the Governor-General Sir [John Kerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerr_(governor-general) "John Kerr (governor-general)") and the subsequent reintroduction of knighthoods as part of the order.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4) White later wrote that Kerr's behaviour "moved me farther to the Left and made me a convinced Republican."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991602-50) Over the following years, he would break with numerous long-term friends because he thought they supported the conservative establishment or had compromised their personal or artistic integrity.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991578,_612%E2%80%9315-51)

In November 1975 the young theatre director [Jim Sharman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Sharman "Jim Sharman") approached White to discuss a revival of _The Season at Sarsaparilla._ They also agreed to film his story "The Night the Prowler" and White began working on a script. The meeting sparked a revival in White's interest in theatre and a long-term working relationship between the two men.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991559%E2%80%9362-52)

In 1976 White was working on a new novel, _The Twyborn Affair,_ partly based on aspects of his own life and that of male Antarctic explorer [Herbert Dyce-Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Dyce_Murphy "Herbert Dyce Murphy") (1879–1971) who had lived as a woman for several years. In researching his novel, White revisited the regions of New South Wales where White had lived and worked as a youth, and significant locations in London, France and Greece. In October, _A Fringe of Leaves_ was published to generally favourable reviews and sold well. Sharman's production of _A Season at Sarsaparilla_ in Sydney was also a critical success and attracted good audiences.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991562%E2%80%9371-53)

In 1977 a project to film _Voss_ with [Joseph Losey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Losey "Joseph Losey") as director collapsed when the promoter Harry Miller failed to gain finance. Miller eventually sold the film rights to Nolan. The success of _The Season at Sarsaparilla_ had inspired White to write his first play in over 12 years, _Big Toys_, about plutocracy and corruption in Sydney. The play, directed by Sharman, premiered in Sydney in October but attracted generally unfavourable reviews and moderate audiences.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991572%E2%80%9377-54)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Patrick_White_1972.jpg/250px-Patrick_White_1972.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Patrick_White_1972.jpg)

White in 1972

The film of _The Night the Prowler_, directed by Sharman, premiered at the _Sydney Film Festival_ in June 1978. Reviews were generally unfavourable and the film failed at the box office.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991578%E2%80%9381,_589-55) Sharman's 1979 production of _A Cheery Soul_ for the [Sydney Theatre Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Theatre_Company "Sydney Theatre Company") broke box office records for the drama theatre of the Opera House despite mixed reviews. _The Twyborn Affair_ was published in Britain in November 1979 to very positive reviews and became a best seller. The response from critics and the public in the United States was more subdued.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991588,_591-56)

In October 1979 White started work on a memoir, _Flaws in the Glass_, in which he planned to write publicly for the first time about his homosexuality and his relationship with Manoly Lascaris. The book was published in Britain in October 1981 to great publicity and became his biggest seller in his life time. Much of the publicity stemmed from his scathing character portraits of Nolan, Kerr and [Joan Sutherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Sutherland "Joan Sutherland"). Nolan considered suing White for defamation and their friendship ended.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991592%E2%80%9395,_602%E2%80%93607-57)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

The 1982 [Adelaide Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide_Festival "Adelaide Festival") was directed by Sharman who had commissioned a new play by White, _Signal Driver_. The festival also featured a short excerpt from an opera based on _Voss._ The opera had been commissioned by [Opera Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_Australia "Opera Australia") with [Richard Meale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Meale "Richard Meale") as composer and [David Malouf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Malouf "David Malouf") the librettist. Critics were generally lukewarm towards _Signal Driver_, but encouraging towards the fragment of Voss. White, in contrast, disliked Meale's approach to _Voss_ but was enthusiastic about the production of _Signal Driver_.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991610-58) White was encouraged to write a new play for Sharman, _Netherwood_, "about the sanity in insanity and the insanity in sanity". The play premiered in Adelaide in May 1983 but attracted hostile reviews which White considered a deliberate media campaign to sabotage his work.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991610%E2%80%9311,_616-59)

By 1984 White had become disillusioned with the [Hawke Labor government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawke_government "Hawke government") and publicly and financially supported the new [Nuclear Disarmament Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Disarmament_Party "Nuclear Disarmament Party"). White had been publicly campaigning for nuclear disarmament since 1981, calling it: "the most important moral issue in history."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991611%E2%80%9312,_618-60)

### Late work and declining health

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Late work and declining health")]

In late 1984 White was hospitalised due to osteoporosis, crumbled vertebrae and glaucoma resulting from his long-term use of cortisone to treat his asthma and chest infections. Although he was still mentally agile, his physical health and mobility were declining.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991619%E2%80%9320-61)

He had recovered sufficiently by January 1985 to recommence work on a new novel, _Memoirs of Many in One,_ which he described as a "religious" and "bawdy" novel about senility. Posing as the editor of the memoirs of Alex Xenophon Demirjian Gray, White felt free to explore various aspects of his own character. The novel was published in Britain on 1 April 1986 and sharply divided critics.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991622%E2%80%9324,_628-62)

[Salman Rushdie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salman_Rushdie "Salman Rushdie") wrote to White in 1985, praising the novel _Voss:_ "I cannot think when last a book so moved me."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-63) By this time, however, White was tired of praise for the novel as he rated several of his other works more highly.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes20142%E2%80%934-64) The completed opera _Voss_ opened at the Adelaide Festival in March 1986 to general critical acclaim. White, however, boycotted the premiere because the festival had invited the Queen to attend. He attended the Sydney premiere later that year and judged it: "a stupendous occasion."[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991629-65)

In April 1987 White's new play, _Shepherd on the Rocks,_ opened at Adelaide in a production directed by Neil Armfield. White attended and deemed it a success.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991631-66) He had also written three short prose poems which were published as _Three Uneasy Pieces_ in late 1987 _._ White was determined that none of his works would be published or performed in 1988 which was the [bicentenary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Bicentenary "Australian Bicentenary") of British settlement in Australia.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4) He also urged a boycott of all official celebrations of the event, stating: "circuses don't solve serious problems."[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991632%E2%80%9364-67)

White was hospitalised with pneumonia in August 1988. A nurse stayed at his home for the remainder of his life and he no longer had the strength to attend protest rallies.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991636%E2%80%9340-68) In June 1989, a selection of his public statements, speeches and interviews was published as _Patrick White Speaks_. In October, the Sydney Theatre Company staged a successful revival of _The Ham Funeral_ directed by Neil Armfield. White attended the premiere in his last public appearance.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991640%E2%80%9342-69)

In July 1990 White contracted pleurisy and suffered a bronchial collapse. He refused to be hospitalised and died at home at dawn on 30 September.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991643%E2%80%9344-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr2008-71)

## Religious and political views

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Religious and political views")]

### Religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Religion")]

White was raised an Anglican but stated, "I… went through my youth believing in nothing but my own ego."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991284-72) In late 1951 he experienced a religious conversion:

> If I say I had no religious tendencies between adolescence and _The Tree of Man_, it's because I was sufficiently vain and egotistical to feel one can ignore certain realities. (I think the turning point came during a season of unending rain at Castle Hill when I fell flat on my back one day in the mud and starting cursing a God I had convinced myself didn't exist. My personal scheme of things until then at once seemed too foolish to continue holding.)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan19805-73)

As the 1950s progressed White became disillusioned with the Anglican church and his religious beliefs became more eclectic.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991357%E2%80%9358,_451%E2%80%9352-74) He once described himself as a "lapsed Anglican egotist agnostic pantheist occultist existentialist would-be though failed Christian Australian."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-:02-75) White stated in 1981 that he did not call himself a Christian because he could not follow Christ's injunction to forgive.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-:02-75) In 1969, however, he had affirmed the importance of religion in his work: "Religion. Yes, that's behind all my books. What I am interested in is the relationship between the blundering human being and God."[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-76)

### Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Politics")]

In the 1930s White was not politically engaged, but was sympathetic to the [Francoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francoist_Spain "Francoist Spain") cause in the [Spanish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War") and supported Britain's policy of [appeasing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appeasement "Appeasement") Hitler.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991164%E2%80%9365,_172%E2%80%9375-77) He later expressed regret over his complacency regarding European fascism.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas2024165%E2%80%9367-78) On his return to Australia after the Second World War he had little interest in politics but routinely voted for the [conservative coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_(Australia) "Coalition (Australia)") in elections.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991491-79) He became involved in politics in 1969 when he joined protests against the Vietnam war and conscription of Australian troops for the conflict. He also supported the trade union [Green Bans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_ban "Green ban") against development proposals which threatened the urban environment. He publicly supported the [Australian Labor Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Labor_Party "Australian Labor Party") in the federal elections of 1972, 1974 and 1975 despite a falling out with the prime minister [Gough Whitlam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gough_Whitlam "Gough Whitlam") over sand mining on [Fraser Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K'gari "K'gari").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

Following the dismissal of the Whitlam government in November 1975, he became a prominent advocate for an Australian republic.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991557%E2%80%9358-80) He was a public supporter of Aboriginal self-determination and privately donated money towards Aboriginal education.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWildeHootonAndrews1994-81) From 1981 he became a leading public figure in campaigns for nuclear disarmament and continued his support for various environmental causes. Marr states that a common thread running through his political interventions was his opposition to [plutocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutocracy "Plutocracy").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991611%E2%80%9312,_616-82) Academic Martin Thomas argues that White was acutely aware of his own privileged upbringing and this drove his later concern about social injustice.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas2024165%E2%80%9367-78)

## Critical reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Critical reception")]

White's first published novel, _Happy Valley_ (1939), received favourable reviews in Britain and Australia, although some critics noted that it was too derivative of Joyce, Lawrence and Woolf. The novel was awarded the Gold Medal of the Australian Literature Society.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan198014%E2%80%9315-83)_The Living and the Dead_ (1941) and _The Aunt's Story_ (1948) attracted little critical attention in Australia, although the latter was favourably reviewed in the _New York Times Review of Books_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes20147%E2%80%938-84)

_The Tree of Man_ (1955) was White's first major international success, attracting positive reviews in the United States and the United Kingdom. James Stern, writing in the _New York Times Book Review,_ praised the novel as "a timeless work of art." Australian reviewers were more divided, poet [A. D. Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._D._Hope "A. D. Hope") calling White's prose "pretentious and illiterate verbal sludge." The novel sold eight thousand copies in Australia in the first three months and was awarded the Gold Medal of the Australian Literature Society.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201415%E2%80%9316-85)

_Voss_ (1957) was reviewed favourably in the United Kingdom but critics in the United States and Australia were more ambivalent. A significant body of Australian critics continued to fault White's prose style and some objected to his rejection of the realist prose tradition.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201417%E2%80%9318-86) The novel was a best seller in the United Kingdom and won the inaugural Australian Miles Franklin Award. _Riders in the Chariot_ (1961) also achieved critical and commercial success in the United Kingdom, and won admiring reviews in Australia.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

By 1963 White was widely accepted as the major Australian literary novelist. A. D. Hope called him "unquestionably the best known and most discussed novelist of the day" and thought his success was "indicative of a break with the naturalistic tradition which has dominated Australian fiction since the turn of the century, and may well be a portent of a more imaginative and a more intellectual sort of fiction."[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes201418-87) White was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1973. Academic Elizabeth Webby states that many critics consider _The Twyborn Affair_ the best of his subsequent work.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

Katherine Brisbane states that the reception of White's plays has been ambivalent as they mix realism, expressionism and poetic and vernacular dialogue in a way which has challenged audiences and directors.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrisbane2009393%E2%80%9394-88)_The Ham Funeral_ (1947) was successfully produced in 1962 after it was rejected by the Adelaide Festival for obscenity. It was successfully revived in 1989. _The Season at Sarsaparilla_ (1962) has been his most produced play.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4)

## Themes and style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Themes and style")]

### Themes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Themes")]

According to critic Brian Kiernan, "the basic situation in his [White's] fiction is the attempt of individuals, most often individuals alienated from society, to grasp some higher, more essential reality that lies beyond or behind social existence."[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan19801-89) The search for a higher reality is most often presented as an exploration of various forms of religious or mystical experience[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams199374,_159-90) and the "seers" are variously pioneer-settlers (_The Tree of Man_), explorers (_Voss_), artists (_The Vivisector_), the simple-minded (_The Solid Mandala_), those fleeing into the self (_The Aunt's Story_) or those on the margins of society. Sexual ambivalence and the search for personal identity are also recurrent themes that become more prominent in the later novels.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams1993142-91)

Society, in particular Australian society, is mostly portrayed as materialistic, conformist and life-inhibiting.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan19805,_67,_136-92) White satirises what he called in 1958, "The Great Australian Emptiness"

> in which the mind is the least of possessions, in which the rich man is the important man, in which the schoolmaster and the journalist rule what intellectual roost there is, in which beautiful youths and girls stare at life through blind blue eyes, in which human teeth fall like autumn leaves, the buttocks of cars grow hourly glassier, food means cake and steak, muscles prevail, and the march of material ugliness does not raise a quiver from the average nerves."[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan19806-93)

The academic Mark Williams argues that White places the religious impulse at the centre of the human condition and his work, adding that "religion is one of the central values, along with art and love, which he considers to be denigrated in his homeland."[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams199374-94) Kiernan notes a division among critics over whether "he is essentially a simple and traditional writer who affirms a religious, even mystical view of life, or one who is distinctively modern, sophisticated and ironic, continually exploring transcendent possibilities but with detachment and even scepticism."[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan19802-95) Greg Clarke argues that Christian discourse is central to White's writing.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-:02-75)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-:1-96) Marr, Williams and Kiernan, however, state that White drew on various religious and mystical traditions in his work including Judaism, [Jungian archetypes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jungian_archetypes "Jungian archetypes") and [gnosticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnosticism "Gnosticism").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarr1991451%E2%80%9352-97)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams1993147-98)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan1980107-99)

### Style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Style")]

White's early novels were heavily influenced by the modernism of Eliot, Joyce, Lawrence and Woolf.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan198015-100)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams199313%E2%80%9314,_19-101) Kiernan has called his mature work "complex, ambiguous and ironic verbal structures".[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan1980138-102) His narratives shift seamlessly between past and present, inner experience and outer awareness, and the point of view of different characters.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan198093-103)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams1993167-104) According to Williams, "the point of view of the narrative in any White novel changes continually, rapidly and disconcertingly. The narrative voice ... is a voice composed of many voices, a slippery, complex, fluent medium."[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams1993167-104)

White frequently shifts between tones, styles and linguistic [registers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_(sociolinguistics) "Register (sociolinguistics)").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams1993167-104) According to Kiernan, "A self-conscious play with conventions, a parodic playfulness, is apparent through White's adoption of various modes in his work from the first."[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan198043-105) His transitions between realist, expressionist, symbolist and romantic modes[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan198028,_32,_54-106)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams19936,_46%E2%80%9349-107) were a conscious attempt to demonstrate that "the Australian novel is not necessarily the dreary, dun-coloured offspring of journalistic realism."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4) Kiernan states that in _Voss_ the theme of the outsider as visionary explorer of the human condition is undercut by ironic comedy and parodies of the "gothic excess" of romantic literature.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKiernan198055%E2%80%9357-108) Williams argues that White's tendency for parody and playfulness become more prominent in later works such as _The Twyborn Affair_ and _Memoirs of Many in One._ The tone becomes less portentous and more relaxed, and the works more self-referential.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams1993140%E2%80%9342,_147-109)

## Influence and legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Patrick_White&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Influence and legacy")]

Critic Susan Lever considers White a pivotal figure in Australian literature, stating that he made the novel, rather than poetry, the pre-eminent literary form. He "transformed the possibilities of the Australian novel by demonstrating that it was a place to test ideas against complex spiritual, psychological and emotional experience, not only an avenue for national storytelling."[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTELever2009498-110)

Australian novelists influenced by White include [Thomas Keneally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Keneally "Thomas Keneally"), [Thea Astley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thea_Astley "Thea Astley"), [Randolph Stow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_Stow "Randolph Stow") and [Christopher Koch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Koch "Christopher Koch"). Lever argues that the following generations of novelists were more influenced by recent trends in world literature. Novelist [David Malouf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Malouf "David Malouf") states that White's "High Modernism" is a literary form that has become unfashionable but that this could change.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTELever2009500,_504%E2%80%9306-111) In 2018, novelist [Christos Tsiolkas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christos_Tsiolkas "Christos Tsiolkas") argued that White was an important figure in Australian literature who hadn't received enough attention in recent decades.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-112) Writing in 2024, critic Martin Thomas noted that critical and public interest in White had declined.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas2024155-113)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Patrick_White_Lawns.jpg/250px-Patrick_White_Lawns.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Patrick_White_Lawns.jpg)

The Patrick White Lawns with temporary stage, March 2015.

The [Patrick White Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White_Award "Patrick White Award") is an annual literary prize which White founded in 1975 with the prize money from his Nobel prize. It is awarded to writers who have made a significant contribution to Australian literature.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-114) The Patrick White Indigenous Writers Award is for Indigenous students in New South Wales from Kindergarten to year 12. It is run by the Aboriginal Education Council which was a beneficiary of Patrick White's estate.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-115) The Sydney Theatre Company sponsors the [Patrick White Playwrights Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White_Playwrights'_Award "Patrick White Playwrights' Award") and Fellowship in honour of White's contribution to Australian theatre.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-116)

In 2006 the National Library of Australia acquired a large quantity of White's manuscripts. These included an unfinished novel, _The Hanging Garden,_ which was published in 2012. The Art Gallery of New South Wales owns a 1940 portrait of White by de Maistre, and Parliament House, Sydney, owns a 1980 portrait by [Brett Whiteley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Whiteley "Brett Whiteley").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebby2012-4) A portrait of White by [Louis Kahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Kahan "Louis Kahan") won the 1962 [Archibald Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Prize "Archibald Prize").[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-117) White donated much of his own collection of Australian art to the Art Gallery of New South Wales.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWildeHootonAndrews1994-81)

As of 2024 there is no museum or institution dedicated to White's life and work. His former residence, "Dogwoods", at Castle Hill is privately owned but has a commemorative plaque and the surrounding streets are named after him. His former Sydney residence at Centennial Park is privately owned but is heritage listed.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas2024169-118) White is commemorated by the Patrick White Lawns adjacent to the [National Library of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Library_of_Australia "National Library of Australia") in Canberra.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-119)

In 2006 a [hoaxer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_hoax "Literary hoax") submitted a chapter of White's novel _The Eye of the Storm_ to a dozen Australian publishers under the name Wraith Picket (an anagram of White's name). All of the publishers rejected the manuscript and none recognised it as White's work.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas2024155-113)

In 2010 White's novel _The Vivisector_ was shortlisted for the [Lost Man Booker Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Man_Booker_Prize "Lost Man Booker Prize") for 1970.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-120) In 2011 [Fred Schepisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Schepisi "Fred Schepisi")'s film adaptation of the novel _[The Eye of the Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Eye\_of\_the\_Storm\_(2011\_film) "The Eye of the Storm (2011 film)")_ won The Age Critics Award for the best Australian feature at the Melbourne International Film Festival.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_White#cite_note-121)

British literary award
